title: We Removed the Shopping Cart Corrals. Then We Called the Customers Lazy. Education
author: Stinehart, Kevin
summary: Stinehart uses a parking lot observation -- carts piled on curbs at a store with few corrals, all returned at the adjacent store with abundant corrals -- to argue that school behavior problems are systems problems, not character problems. Drawing on education systems improvement science (Carnegie Foundation) and developmental research on play, he contends that schools have removed the inputs (recess, unstructured play, movement) that build executive function -- the very capacities they then demand from students throughout the day. His school's Play Club reduced physical aggression incidents from 65 to 32 and cut office referrals for defiance in half. The cruelest irony: schools punish dysregulated students by removing recess -- taking away the developmental tool that would build the regulation they lack. Stinehart closes with practical diagnostic questions: where does behavior fall apart, what have we asked children to do in the hour before, and what does our schedule make 'easy' versus 'hard'?
points: A system produces exactly the outcomes it is designed to produce: when the same behaviors consistently appear across students at the same time under the same conditions, that is information about the environment, not a character flaw in the children.

Play is not a reward for completing real learning -- it is the primary engine of executive function development, building working memory, self-regulation, conflict resolution, and resilience that make everything else in school possible.

Stinehart's Play Club (90 minutes of unstructured outdoor play after school) reduced physical aggression by 51%, eliminated verbal threats, and cut defiance referrals in half -- without a new program, curriculum, or initiative.

The most self-defeating school discipline practice is removing recess as a consequence for dysregulation: it removes the developmental input that would build the regulation the student lacks, guaranteeing the cycle continues.

Designing schools around students least likely to be harmed by poor design is not neutral -- it is a policy choice that systematically disadvantages the students who most need well-designed conditions.
quotes: We removed the cart corrals. Then we started blaming the customers for being lazy. A system produces exactly the outcomes it is designed to produce. If you want to understand why an outcome keeps happening, stop staring at the outcome. Start studying the system underneath it.

Play is the primary engine of that development. Not a break from it. Not a reward for getting through the 'real stuff.' Free play is the most powerful builder of working memory, self-regulation, conflict resolution, cooperation, and resilience that childhood has.

We gave them a seven-hour school day with ever-shrinking recess, vanishing time to communicate and move, and an ever-growing list of difficult cognitive and behavioral demands. Then we wondered why they put the cart on the curb.

You know what's most painful about all of this? We punish dysregulated kids by removing recess. We take away the very developmental tool that would help them build regulation. We make them sit longer, move less, and connect less -- because they couldn't sit still, move less, and connect less.

Dr. Peter Gray has tracked the data across five decades: 'as play declines, emotional fragility, anxiety, and depression rise.' It isn't a coincidence. It's a system producing the outcomes it was built to produce.
We are not facing a generation of bad children. We are facing a generation of children operating inside bad system design.
The children aren't lazy. The cart corrals are difficult to get to.
